data.text: Luxury boutiques, high-end residences and luxury hotels ask very different things of metal surface finishing, yet they share one underlying logic: pre-treatment decides adhesion, process parameters decide texture, and process control decides batch consistency. This guide breaks spray coating, polishing, brushing and electroplating down to the sub-process level, with a scene selection matrix, parameter gradients, equipment configuration, inspection methods and defect prevention.
Headline figures for the whole system:

items: Core processes: 4 — spray · polish · brush · electroplate

data.text: 1. The Four Surface Treatment Processes at a Glance

Spray for colour, polishing for gloss, brushing for texture, plating for performance. The four processes can be used alone or stacked in combination — selection depends on the base material, the scene and the budget, but the pre-treatment logic and quality-control principles are the same.

data.caption: Spray booth in the field: an operator spraying an aluminium panel with an electrostatic gun

data.text: Atomised paint is sprayed onto the metal surface to form a continuous coating. Strong colour capability across the full matte-to-gloss range — the workhorse process for aluminium panels and shaped parts.

data.caption: 8K mirror-polished stainless steel: distortion-free reflection

data.text: Microscopic peaks are removed mechanically or chemically to lower roughness. From matte satin to an 8K mirror, the polish grade directly decides the metal's sense of quality.

data.caption: Long-grain brushed stainless steel panel: directional hairline texture

data.text: Abrasives scratch the surface in a controlled direction to form a regular pattern. Brushing hides fine scratches, cuts reflection and adds tactile depth — the most widely used metal texture process for residences and hotels.

data.caption: PVD gold titanium coated panel: hard metallic colour finish

data.text: A metal layer is deposited by electrolysis or vacuum coating. PVD titanium coating gives gold, black titanium, rose gold and other colours with high hardness and wear and corrosion resistance — the first choice for luxury boutiques.

Key point: the four processes are not interchangeable. Spray changes colour, polish changes gloss, brush changes texture and plate changes performance — pick the property you actually need before you pick the process.
2. The Gloss Scale and Process Usage Split

Gloss is the first thing the eye reads, and it is the parameter most often left unquantified on drawings. Measured in 60° gloss units (GU), higher values reflect more. Luxury boutiques take the high range, high-end residences the mid-to-low range, and hotels grade it zone by zone.

data.caption: Gloss scale sample panels: from matte shot-blasted to 8K mirror

data.text: Gloss scale, physical samples — left to right: matte shot-blasted 12 GU · brushed 30–55 GU · satin 68 GU · 8K mirror 96 GU. Gloss and roughness Ra correspond one to one; boutiques take the high end, residences the mid-to-low end, hotels grade by zone.

data.caption: Four finished panels side by side: spray coated, mirror polished, brushed and PVD plated

data.text: Actual usage frequency of the four processes, sampled across mid-to-high-end architectural metal finishing projects.
Key point: brushing is the most used process overall, but usage split is not the same as budget split — PVD plating is the smallest share by area and the largest by cost.

The heart of spraying is not the spraying but the pre-treatment and curing. Coating adhesion, colour difference and weatherability depend seven-tenths on thorough pre-treatment and a precise cure curve. Broken down below from substrate pre-treatment to finished-part inspection.

Atomised paint is attached evenly to the metal surface, then levelled and cured into a continuous coating. Suited to aluminium panels, shaped parts and large facades, with the full colour range from matte to gloss and from plain to metallic. Common types: fluorocarbon (PVDF), powder and ceramic coating.

items: 01-1 Alkaline degreasing — alkaline degreaser pH 9–11 · 50–60 ℃ · soak / spray 3–5 min · rinse to conductivity ≤ 50 μS/cm
01-2 Acid pickling — nitric / sulfuric mixed acid · room temperature 2–5 min · removes scale and rust · two rinse stages
01-3 Chromating / chromate-free passivation — chromate bath Cr³⁺ 0.5–2 g/L · 25–35 ℃ · 1–3 min · forms a nanoscale conversion film
01-4 DI-water rinse & drying — DI-water rinse conductivity ≤ 10 μS/cm · drying 80–120 ℃ / 10–15 min · no water marks · into the dust-free booth
02-1 Primer spray — epoxy primer film 5–10 μm · gun distance 150–250 mm · atomising pressure 0.3–0.5 MPa · even coverage, no misses
04-1 Topcoat spray — fluorocarbon / powder film 25–40 μm · spray environment 20–28 ℃ / 45–65% RH · thin multi-pass spraying 2–3 passes · colour difference ΔE ≤ 1.0
Pre-treatment is everything — incomplete degreasing causes blistering and peeling. The line must run degrease → rinse → chromate → DI rinse with conductivity ≤ 10 μS/cm.
Layered film control — primer 5–10 μm and topcoat 25–40 μm; too thick sags, too thin lacks hiding power.
Same-batch colour control — one colour code must be sprayed in one batch, with every panel colorimeter-checked to ΔE ≤ 1.0.
Cure-curve records — oven temperature curves must be archived; too fast a ramp causes pinholes and orange peel.
Booth cleanliness — the booth must be positive-pressure dust-free with particles ≤ 1000/m³, or the coating shows specks.
Jig management — jigs need regular cleaning; residual coating affects conductivity and earthing, giving uneven film build.
Pre-treatment line — degreasing / pickling tanks · chromate / DI-rinse tanks · drying oven
Spray equipment — electrostatic / air spray guns · reciprocators / robots · positive-pressure dust-free booth
Curing equipment — tunnel curing oven · oven temperature tracker · cooling zone

data.text: Polishing is a subtractive process — microscopic peaks are removed by step-by-step grinding. From coarse grinding to mirror, every grade must fully remove the previous grade's marks or a haze remains. Polish grades from matte to 8K mirror directly decide the metal's sense of quality.

Abrasives or chemical action lower the surface roughness to give a mirror or satin finish. Mechanical polishing steps through belts, sisal wheels and cloth wheels; electrolytic polishing dissolves electrochemically for a uniform mirror.

items: 01-1 Coarse grinding — belt #120–#240 · belt speed 15–25 m/s · removes weld marks and deep scratches · direction perpendicular to the next grade
02-1 Medium grinding — belt #400–#800 · pressure 0.2–0.5 MPa · removes coarse-grind marks · even surface, no patches
03-1 Fine grinding — belt / paper #1000–#2000 · wet or oil grinding · uniform matte surface · prepares for buffing
04-1 Sisal buffing — sisal wheel Ø 200–300 mm · speed 2000–2500 rpm · compound W20–W10 · removes fine-grind marks
05-1 Cloth-wheel finishing — cloth wheel Ø 250–350 mm · speed 2500–3000 rpm · compound W5–W1 · achieves the mirror
06-1 Cleaning & inspection — ultrasonic cleaning with neutral detergent · profilometer Ra check · gloss meter GU check · visual check for haze / rings
Step through every grit — each new belt must fully remove the previous grade's marks, or the mirror shows haze or rings.
Alternate direction — grind each grade perpendicular to the last so you can see at a glance whether it is ground through.
Temperature control — excessive pressure overheats the surface locally, yellowing stainless steel and oxidising copper.
Electropolishing — ideal for complex shaped parts and gives a uniform mirror, but current density and electrolyte temperature must be controlled.
Buffing wheel care — cloth wheels need regular dressing; an uneven wheel face causes waviness.
Clean immediately — clean straight after polishing; residual compound corrodes the surface.
Grinding equipment — wide-belt sander · surface grinder · belt grinder
Polishing equipment — buffing lathes / automatic lines · sisal / cloth / wool wheels · automatic compound spraying
Electropolishing — electrolytic tank / rectifier · temperature control system · cathode plates / jigs

data.text: Brushing forms texture by directional abrasive scratching. Grain direction, coarseness and depth decide the final look — long grain is continuous, short grain is fine, snow-fine gives a random pattern. Brushing hides fine scratches, cuts reflection and adds tactile depth.

Belts, non-woven pads or wire brushes scratch the metal surface directionally to form regular or random micro-texture — the most widely used metal texture process for premium residences and hotels. Grain grades include coarse, fine, long, short and snow-fine.

items: Step 04 · Grain unifying — non-woven pad / nylon wheel
Step 06 · Film protection — PE film / AF coating
01-1 Substrate cleaning — wipe with neutral detergent · removes oil and fingerprints · compressed-air dusting · surface dry, no water marks
02-1 Coarse grain setting — belt #120–#240 · belt speed 12–20 m/s · feed rate 3–8 m/min · sets grain direction and depth
03-1 Fine grain refining — belt #320–#600 · lowers surface roughness · finer, more even grain · direction matches the coarse pass
04-1 Grain unifying — non-woven pad / nylon wheel · removes belt seams · grain depth 0.5–3 μm · gloss 30–55 GU
05-1 Surface cleaning — removes swarf and dust · wipe with neutral detergent · blown dry with compressed air · check grain evenness
06-1 Film protection — PE protective film 50–80 μm · anti-fingerprint coating 1–3 μm · corner guards on all four edges · avoid stacking damage
One grain direction — every panel on the same elevation must be brushed in the same direction, or reflections clash badly at different angles.
Seam transition — grain on adjacent panels must flow across the joint; the texture must not break at the seam.
Belt wear management — belts must be replaced at end of life, or the grain gets shallower and colour difference appears.
Anti-fingerprint coating — an AF coating after brushing stops fingerprints — standard for premium residences and hotels.
Even pressure — brushing pressure must stay constant; pressure fluctuation gives uneven grain depth.
Clean thoroughly — all swarf must be removed after brushing; residual dust harms later coating adhesion.

Abrasives & consumables — belts #120–#600 · non-woven pad / nylon wheel · wire brushes / grinding wheels

data.text: Electroplating deposits a functional layer by electrolysis or vacuum coating. PVD titanium coating gives gold, black titanium, rose gold and other colours with high hardness, wear and corrosion resistance — the first choice for luxury boutiques. Broken down below along the wet-plating and vacuum-coating routes.

Plating splits into wet electroplating and vacuum coating (PVD). PVD titanium is deposited by target sputtering in vacuum: film 0.3–0.5 μm, hardness HV 1500–2500, in gold, champagne, black titanium, rose gold and blue titanium. Anodising is mainly for aluminium, giving a wear- and weather-resistant oxide film.

items: Step 01 · Pre-treatment cleaning — degrease → pickle → DI rinse
Step 04 · Film deposition — target sputtering / arc evaporation
01-1 Ultrasonic degreasing — alkaline degreaser pH 9–11 · 50–60 ℃ · ultrasonic 3–5 min · two rinse stages
01-2 Acid activation — weak-acid soak 1–3 min · removes the oxide film · activates the surface · DI-water rinse
01-3 DI-water rinse & drying — DI-water rinse conductivity ≤ 10 μS/cm · drying 80–120 ℃ · transfer in dust-free conditions · dew point ≤ −40 ℃
03-1 Ion bombardment cleaning — Ar ion bombardment · vacuum level ≤ 5×10⁻³ Pa · bias voltage 300–800 V · time 5–15 min
04-1 Film deposition — targets Ti / Cr / Zr · arc current 60–120 A · deposition temperature 150–450 ℃ · film 0.3–0.5 μm
06-1 Inspection & film — thickness gauge 0.3–0.5 μm · colorimeter ΔE ≤ 1.0 · cross-cut adhesion class 0 · PE film protection
Pre-treatment decides adhesion — eight out of ten PVD failures come from incomplete pre-treatment. Multi-stage ultrasonic cleaning is mandatory, with DI-rinse conductivity ≤ 10 μS/cm.
One furnace, one colour — one colour code must be coated in one furnace run; target wear shifts colour, so targets need scheduled replacement.
Film uniformity — parts must rotate in the chamber so all faces coat evenly, deviation ≤ ±15%.
Colour-difference control — keep a colour board per furnace and colorimeter-sample panels; deliver only at ΔE ≤ 1.0.
Target management — targets must be replaced at end of life, or film composition drifts and colour shifts.
Cooling rate — vacuum-cool below 60 ℃ before opening the furnace; quenching cracks the film.
Pre-treatment equipment — ultrasonic cleaning line · DI-rinse tank · drying oven
Vacuum coating equipment — multi-arc ion plating furnace · magnetron sputtering furnace · vacuum pump set
Anodising equipment — electrolytic tank / rectifier · temperature control system · sealing line

data.text: Surface treatment quality cannot be judged by eye alone. Below are the inspection items, instruments and acceptance criteria for the four processes; agree the inspection plan at the sample-sealing stage.

items: Gloss — gloss meter 60° · checked against sealed samples
Visual check — haze / rings / waviness · no visible defects
Reflection test — mirror face-on, no distortion · no funfair-mirror effect
Surface cleaning — no compound residue · no oil or fingerprints
Grain direction — visual check · one direction per elevation
Grain uniformity — visual + raking light · no uneven depth
Anti-fingerprint coating — film 1–3 μm · fingerprint wipe test
Adhesion — cross-cut · class 0; no flaking in bend test
Wear resistance — rub tester · 1000 cycles at 500 g, no breakthrough
Colour difference — colorimeter · ΔE within spec vs sealed samples
Packing — PE film intact · corner guards · scannable QR
Batch consistency — same-batch sampling · ΔE / film / gloss
Wastewater treatment — neutralisation · heavy-metal precipitation · compliant discharge
Exhaust gas treatment — activated-carbon adsorption + catalytic combustion
Hazardous waste — sorted collection · compliant disposal · full records

data.caption: Coating thickness measurement: magnetic, eddy-current and X-ray gauges
Colour difference comparison: checked against sealed samples under a D65 source
Gloss measurement: 60° gloss meter
Cross-hatch adhesion test: class 0 is the pass grade
Environment and safety: wastewater and exhaust gas treatment facilities

data.text: Inspection principles — surface treatment quality must be judged against the sealed samples, compared under a D65 standard light source. Colorimeters, thickness gauges, profilometers and gloss meters are the four mandatory instruments; adhesion, salt spray and abrasion are type-test items, sampled every batch. All inspection data must be recorded and archived as the basis for acceptance and after-sales traceability.
9. Common Surface Treatment Defects and Prevention

These twelve problems account for over 90% of after-sales complaints in metal surface finishing. Spotting the causes and defending early in the process costs an order of magnitude less than reworking afterwards.
Incomplete degreasing, an incomplete chromate film, or insufficient cure temperature or time leave adhesion below spec.

items: Prevention — multi-stage ultrasonic cleaning with DI-rinse conductivity ≤ 10 μS/cm; cure curves recorded and archived; cross-cut class 0 before delivery

data.text: Gun too close, film too thick, thinner flashing off too fast, or ambient temperature too high — the coating levels poorly.

items: Prevention — gun distance 150–250 mm; control film by multi-pass spraying; 20–28 ℃ and 45–65% RH

data.text: Poor booth cleanliness, jigs shedding old coating, or poorly filtered paint put particles in the film.

items: Prevention — positive-pressure dust-free booth with particles ≤ 1000/m³; clean jigs regularly; filter paint through 100–150 mesh

data.text: Previous-grade marks not fully removed when changing grits, or wheel speed and pressure too high, overheating the surface locally.

items: Prevention — step through every grit with direction perpendicular each time; keep speed at 2000–3000 rpm; reflection-test mirrors

data.text: Excessive pressure overheats the surface and oxidises stainless yellow; copper not oxidation-protected straight after polishing.

items: Prevention — control pressure and temperature; apply AF coating or anti-oxidation sealing immediately after polishing

data.text: An uneven wheel face or an undressed cloth wheel puts periodic waves in the surface.

items: Prevention — dress wheel faces regularly; replace cloth wheels at end of life; keep buffing pressure even

data.text: Panels on the same elevation brushed in different directions, or grain not flowing across joints — reflections clash badly at different angles.

items: Prevention — mark grain direction on the fabrication ticket; one direction per elevation; grain must flow across seams

data.text: Belts used past their life give shallower grain; unstable feed speed gives uneven depth.

items: Prevention — log belt hours and replace on schedule; hold feed speed at 3–8 m/min; compare grain depth panel by panel

data.text: No AF coating after brushing, or the coating is too thin, so fingerprints will not wipe off.

items: Prevention — apply 1–3 μm AF coating after brushing; cure it fully; supply neutral detergent and microfibre cloths

data.text: Incomplete pre-treatment cleaning, insufficient vacuum, film too thin, or later attack by strong-alkali or chlorine cleaners.

items: Prevention — multi-stage ultrasonic cleaning with conductivity ≤ 10 μS/cm; vacuum ≤ 5×10⁻³ Pa; film ≥ 0.3 μm; supply a neutral-cleaner list

data.text: Different target wear between furnace runs, temperature fluctuation, or part position in the chamber shift the colour.

items: Prevention — one colour code per furnace run; replace targets on schedule; rotate parts for uniformity; keep a colour board per furnace at ΔE ≤ 1.0

data.text: Parts not rotating, unequal target-to-part distances, or arc-current fluctuation give uneven film across faces.

items: Prevention — rotating jigs; control target-to-part distance; stable arc current; film deviation ≤ ±15%

data.text: Core principle — the final result of surface finishing is decided 70% by pre-treatment, 20% by process parameters and 10% by equipment precision. Spray adhesion, plating bond, mirror quality and brushing uniformity all trace back to thorough pre-treatment and stable parameters. Pre-treatment must be standardised, cure curves recorded and archived, and batch colour difference instrument-checked — all three are indispensable.
